title: FreeToken: Serving Frontier MoE Models on the Machine You Own
hook: Instead of treating a laptop as a tiny datacenter GPU, FreeToken treats the whole machine as one elastic inference platform — and runs a 753B model on a single workstation card.
key_points: Open-weight frontier models exist, but serving stacks still assume datacenter infrastructure.
FreeToken co-designs the full stack: model layout and loading, expert residency, CPU-GPU execution, agentic state reuse, memory management.
Built around two edge realities: agent workloads keep changing their execution pattern, and every machine's resource balance differs.
Rather than fixing an offloading strategy up front, it continuously remaps computation and model state onto whatever is actually free.
Supports 20+ MoE models from an 8GB laptop GPU up to a workstation GPU.
Reported reach: 35B on a laptop, 284B on a gaming desktop, and 753B GLM-5.2 on one workstation GPU.
content_html: Frontier-quality open weights keep landing, but the software that serves them was written for clusters. FreeToken — from a Berkeley/MIT group including Song Han, Matei Zaharia and Ion Stoica — starts from a different premise: a personal machine isn't a small GPU, it's a unified, elastic inference platform with CPU, GPU and memory you can play against each other.
extra_html:
How it works

The system co-designs the whole serving stack — model layout and loading, which experts stay resident, how work splits across CPU and GPU, reuse of agentic state, and runtime memory management — around two facts about local inference. First, agent workloads shift their execution pattern as they run, so a static plan goes stale. Second, no two personal machines have the same resource balance. So instead of committing to a fixed offloading strategy, FreeToken continuously maps computation and model state onto whatever resources are actually available.

Why it matters

The authors report support for more than 20 MoE models and real coding and tool-using agents, across hardware from an 8GB laptop GPU to a single workstation GPU. The headline is what those machines can now practically run: a 35B model on a laptop, a 284B model on a gaming desktop, and the 753B GLM-5.2 on one workstation GPU. That's the difference between open weights being downloadable and being deployable. The system is released at flashml.ai.

flashcards.prompt: What are the two realities of local AI that FreeToken's design is built around?
flashcards.back_html: Agent workloads continuously change their execution pattern, and edge hardware exposes heterogeneous resources whose balance differs from machine to machine.

flashcards.prompt: How does FreeToken differ from a conventional offloading approach?

choices.text: It continuously remaps computation and model state onto currently available resources instead of committing to a fixed strategy
It quantizes experts to 4-bit so the whole model fits in VRAM
It routes hard tokens to a cloud endpoint and easy ones locally

flashcards.explanation_html: The core idea is elasticity: no fixed offloading plan, just continuous mapping onto the resources the machine actually has free at that moment.

flashcards.prompt: Which part of the stack does FreeToken leave untouched?

choices.text: None of it — the paper co-designs layout, expert residency, CPU-GPU execution, state reuse, and memory management
Expert residency, which it inherits from vLLM
Memory management, which it delegates to the OS

flashcards.explanation_html: The contribution is explicitly a full-stack co-design; the pieces only pay off together because they all trade against the same scarce machine resources.
